chip-blocks.alt: Block diagram of the BNO08x: its function blocks, how they connect and which package pins reach each block.
chip-blocks.description: The BNO08x's function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches.

chip-capabilities.title: What the BNO08x does
chip-capabilities.alt: Capability map of the BNO08x: Orientation (supported): Rotation vector, game, geomagnetic, AR/VR stabilised and gyro-integrated quaternions, with accuracy; Motion outputs (supported): Acceleration, linear acceleration, gravity, angular rate and magnetic field, calibrated or raw; Activity and gestures (supported): Step counter, tap, shake, stability, significant motion and activity classifier as events; Rates, batching and timestamps (supported): A report rate per sensor, batched reports flushed on request, each with its own timestamp; Calibration (supported): Dynamic calibration on or off per sensor, saved to flash on request or periodically; Tare and reorientation (supported): Zeroes the heading or the full orientation, or rotates every output to the way the board is mounted; Configuration records (supported): Reads, writes and erases the records in the hub's flash, and each sensor's metadata; Reset, sleep and identity (supported): Resets the hub by pin or command, puts it to sleep and wakes it, and reads the product ID; Firmware update (not covered): The bootloader that writes new hub firmware; the driver never starts it.
chip-capabilities.description: Each card is one function of the BNO08x: an icon, its name and what it does for the application. The filled pill says how this driver covers it (legend below); the outlined pills are the chip registers behind it. The coverage table in the README gives the driver calls and the datasheet section of each card.

chip-circuit-i2c.description: A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected.

chip-hero.title: BNO08x
chip-hero.alt: Overview of the BNO08x, a 9-axis sensor hub in one package: an accelerometer, a gyroscope and a magnetometer with a Cortex-M0+ that runs the sensor fusion and reports finished orientation, motion and activity results to the host. A MCU talks to it over I2C, SPI or UART; it drives H_INTN line; it reads back Motion and magnetic field. Headline figures: 9 axes accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer; 1000 Hz gyro rotation vector; 400 Hz rotation vector; 3.7 ms rotation vector latency at 200 Hz; 3 MHz SPI; I2C 400 kHz, UART 3 Mbit/s; 2.4 to 3.6 V VDD; VDDIO 1.7 to 3.6 V; 5.2 x 3.8 mm LGA-28 body, 1.1 mm high.
chip-hero.description: The BNO08x in the middle, drawn as its LGA-28 package. On the left the MCU that runs the driver, joined to it by I2C, SPI or UART. To the right, what the chip drives, in the order the power flows. Below it, what the chip reads back. The tiles at the bottom are the headline numbers, each with the datasheet section and page it comes from.

driver-layers.title: The layers, one of them yours
driver-layers.alt: Layer diagram: your application calls the Bno08x core, which sends register reads and writes through the I2C, SPI or UART port contract to the port class you write, which drives the chip; the core and the contract are the same on every MCU.
driver-layers.description: Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers.

one-sample-through-the-layers.title: One sample through the layers
one-sample-through-the-layers.alt: One sensor sample: your code enables a feature, the core writes it through your port, the hub pulls its interrupt line low when data is ready, and the next Poll reads, reassembles and decodes the report into an event.
one-sample-through-the-layers.description: Participants, left to right: Your code, Bno08x, Your port and BNO08x. The steps run from top to bottom. Your code sends SetFeature(RotationVector, 10 ms) to Bno08x. Bno08x returns OpId to Your code. Bno08x sends I2cWrite(set feature cargo) to Your port. BNO08x returns H_INTN low to Your port. Your code sends Poll(now) to Bno08x. Bno08x sends IntAsserted(), I2cRead(header, rest) to Your port. A note over Bno08x says: reassemble, timestamp, decode. Bno08x returns Event Sensor on PopEvent() to Your code.

session-states.title: Session states of the driver
session-states.alt: State machine of the BNO08x session with the states Idle, Resetting, WaitAdvert, WaitReady, Ready and Faulted, and the calls and events that move it between them.
session-states.description: Six states. The session starts in Idle. Begin() leaves Idle for Resetting when NRST is wired, for WaitAdvert when it is not, and for Ready on UART-RVC. Resetting goes to WaitAdvert when the reset wait is over. WaitAdvert goes to WaitReady once the advertisement is parsed, and WaitReady goes to Ready when the reset is complete. Ready goes back to WaitReady when the hub restarts. Resetting is also entered by HardReset() and by framing faults. Faulted is reached from Resetting when NRST cannot be released and from WaitAdvert or WaitReady on a start-up timeout, and Begin() or HardReset() lead from Faulted back to Resetting.
